segments.title: Four-funnel liners before Titanic
segments.summary: Titanic and Olympic entered an international four-funnel liner tradition that began with German ships in the late 1890s.
segments.body: Four-funnel liners were already an established prestige type when White Star built Olympic and Titanic. Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse was launched for North German Lloyd in 1897, followed by Deutschland, Kronprinz Wilhelm, Kaiser Wilhelm II, and Kronprinzessin Cecilie. Cunard's Lusitania became the first British example in 1906, followed by Mauretania, Olympic, SS France, Titanic, Aquitania, and Britannic. After World War I, Arundel Castle and Windsor Castle carried the arrangement onto the Africa route rather than transatlantic service. Funnel counts fell as machinery grew more efficient. Their number became a visible clue to a liner's engineering and prestige image.

evidence.note: The transcript traces four-funnel liners from Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse through British, French, and postwar examples.

segments.title: Minas Geraes: armour and turret layout
segments.summary: The Minas Geraes class combined unusually extensive armour with a practical turret arrangement to deter stronger powers.
segments.body: The Minas Geraes class carried armour high above the waterline instead of relying on a narrow belt. Nine inches protected both parts of the central belt, the casemated gun deck, the turrets, and the after conning position, while the forward conning position had twelve inches. Twelve 12-inch guns and twenty-two 4.7-inch guns gave each ship a heavy main and secondary battery. The wing turrets were arranged without assuming unrealistic cross-deck fire. This combination of protection and firepower made the class a costly opponent for any stronger power considering intervention.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the class's layered nine- and twelve-inch armour, heavy armament, restrained use of wing turrets, and deterrent value.

segments.title: Superfiring turrets for export before Royal Navy adoption
segments.summary: Minas Geraes shows that British yards built superfiring layouts for a foreign navy before the Royal Navy adopted them.
segments.body: The Minas Geraes design placed superfiring turrets fore and aft, allowing one turret to fire over another on the centreline. The ships were delivered in 1910, yet the Royal Navy took considerably longer to use superfiring arrangements in its own construction. British yards could offer foreign customers a sensible arrangement that their own navy still treated cautiously. Export orders can therefore reveal design changes that builders implemented abroad before domestic naval institutions accepted them.

evidence.note: The transcript highlights Minas Geraes's forward and aft superfiring turrets and contrasts their export delivery with the Royal Navy's slower adoption of the arrangement.

segments.title: Olympic-class hybrid propulsion
segments.summary: Titanic and Olympic combined familiar reciprocating engines with a low-pressure turbine because relying entirely on the newer technology still looked risky.
segments.body: Olympic and Titanic drove their central four-bladed bronze propeller with a low-pressure turbine, while four-cylinder reciprocating engines powered the two outboard propellers. The plant paired well-understood machinery with one newer, less familiar system. Olympic-class designers chose this cautious mix even during a commercial race for speed. They declined to rely on turbines for the whole propulsion plant. Reliable Atlantic crossings mattered more than theoretical performance gains because a breakdown was worse than a slower passage.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the central low-pressure turbine, reciprocating outboard engines, and the priority of reliable Atlantic service.

segments.title: Delaware's centerline battery and missed speed
segments.summary: USS Delaware shows the clean broadside offered by a centreline battery and the extra speed that might have been possible without the fifth turret.
segments.body: The Delaware class mounted all five main turrets on the centreline. This avoided the compromises of wing turrets and put eight guns on a broadside. Removing the fifth turret would still leave a broadside equal to many contemporary British battleships. The released space might have carried more machinery and produced a faster eight-gun ship closer to a battlecruiser. Delaware used vertical triple-expansion engines while North Dakota had Curtis steam turbines, so the class already tested two machinery choices. A mixed plant like Olympic's or a four-shaft layout offered other possibilities. Cost and design limits kept the ships near 21 knots. The result was a strong hull that never received the extra speed explored by this counterfactual.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Delaware's superfiring centerline turrets, its eight-gun broadside, propulsion alternatives, and unrealized speed potential.

segments.title: The dreadnought race beyond Germany
segments.summary: Royal Navy planners worried about Germany's numbers while watching American and Italian navies for technical ideas.
segments.body: Prewar fleet competition extended beyond the Anglo-German dreadnought race. The Royal Navy watched German ship numbers, while technical developments in the United States and Italy drew closer attention. Delaware shows why: its centreline battery, machinery alternatives, and promising hull offered ideas worth studying even though the class is less familiar than British or German dreadnoughts. A comparison across several navies shows a wider field of experimentation than battleship totals alone suggest.

evidence.note: The transcript says the Royal Navy watched U.S. and Italian technological advances while treating Germany chiefly as a numerical concern.
